pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
> 🔢 **Strand 1 — Number**
Counting, calculating and reasoning with numbers — the language of trade, science and everyday life.

> 🎯 **Content standard** (B8.1.1)
- B8.1.1.1 — Demonstrate understanding and the use of place value for expressing quantities in standard form, rounding numbers and decimals to significant figures and a given number of decimal places. B8.1.1.2 — Apply the concepts and vocabulary of sets to identify perfect squares, determine their square roots and solve real-life problems involving union and intersection of two sets.

> 🎯 **In this chapter you will learn to:**
- read and write numbers greater than one billion in words and figures
- skip count forwards and backwards in 10,000s, 100,000s, 500,000s and other steps
- compare and order whole numbers using >, < and =
- write integers of any size in standard form
- round integers and decimals to a given number of significant figures and decimal places
- solve real-life problems on place value
- use sets to identify perfect squares and find square roots
- solve problems involving the union and intersection of two sets

pages.title: Reading and writing large numbers
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Apply the understanding of place value to read and write number quantities over 1,000,000,000.
Curriculum indicator B8.1.1.1.1
| **B** | **HM** | **TM** | **M** | **HTh** | **TTh** | **Th** | **H** | **T** | **O** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 0 | 2 | 4 | 0 | 8 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 0 |
(B = billions, HM = hundred millions, TM = ten millions, M = millions, HTh = hundred thousands, TTh = ten thousands, Th = thousands, H = hundreds, T = tens, O = ones.) Group the digits in threes from the right (ones, thousands, millions, billions). Read each group, then say its name.
## ✏️ Example 1.1
Write in words: a) 2,408,321 b) the numeral part of the serial number TD1567451 on a currency note c) 3,024,083,210
**Solution**
a) **Two million, four hundred and eight thousand, three hundred and twenty-one.**
b) 1,567,451: **one million, five hundred and sixty-seven thousand, four hundred and fifty-one.**
c) **Three billion, twenty-four million, eighty-three thousand, two hundred and ten.**
## ✏️ Example 1.2
Write in figures: seven billion, three hundred and five million, sixty thousand and forty-two.
**Solution**
**7,305,060,042**

pages.title: Comparing and ordering
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Compare and order whole numbers using >, < and =.
Curriculum indicator B8.1.1.1.3
## ✏️ Example 1.4
a) Find the numbers that are 100,000 more and 1,500,000 less than 98,450,000. b) Insert > or <: 456,789,123 … 456,798,123
**Solution**
a) 98,450,000 + 100,000 = **98,550,000**; 98,450,000 − 1,500,000 = **96,950,000**
b) Compare from the left: 456,7**8**9,123 and 456,7**9**8,123 first differ at the hundred-thousands digit, 8 < 9, so **456,789,123 < 456,798,123**.

pages.title: Standard form
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Express integers of any size in standard form.
Curriculum indicator B8.1.1.1.4
| **Number** | **1** | **10** | **100** | **1,000** | **10,000** | **100,000** | **1,000,000** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Power of 10 | 10^{0} | 10^{1} | 10^{2} | 10^{3} | 10^{4} | 10^{5} | 10^{6} |
> 🔑 **Key idea: Standard form** — A number is in **standard form** (scientific notation) when it is written as **A × 10^{n}**, where **1 ≤ A < 10** and n is an integer. Example: 375 = 3.75 × 10^{2}.
## ✏️ Example 1.5
Write in standard form: a) 10 b) 1,000 c) 26 d) 375 e) 8,765,049 f) 450,000,000
**Solution**
a) 10 = **1 × 10^{1}** b) 1,000 = **1 × 10^{3}**
c) 26 = **2.6 × 10^{1}** d) 375 = **3.75 × 10^{2}**
e) 8,765,049 = **8.765049 × 10^{6}** (the decimal point moves 6 places to the left)
f) 450,000,000 = **4.5 × 10^{8}**
> 🎯 **BECE tip** Count how many places the decimal point moves to make a number between 1 and 10. That count is the power of 10.

pages.title: Word problems on place value
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Create and solve word or real-life problems on place value.
Curriculum indicator B8.1.1.1.6
## ✏️ Example 1.7
Adom earns GH₵2,500 a month after tax and his elder brother Arko earns three times as much. What is their total income after five years if there are no increases in their earnings?
**Solution**
Arko earns 3 × 2,500 = GH₵7,500 a month. Together: 2,500 + 7,500 = GH₵10,000 a month.
Five years = 60 months: 60 × 10,000 = **GH₵600,000** (= 6 × 10^{5} cedis)

pages.title: Sets, perfect squares and square roots
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Use the concept of sets to identify perfect squares and determine the square roots.
Curriculum indicator B8.1.1.2.1
> 🔑 **Key idea: Set** — A **set** is a well-defined collection of objects, called **elements** or **members**, written in curly brackets: A = {2, 4, 6, 8}. "4 ∈ A" means "4 is an element of A".
> 🔑 **Key idea: Perfect square** — A **perfect square** (square number) is the product of a whole number with itself: 1 = 1², 4 = 2², 9 = 3², … The **square root** of a perfect square n is the number which, multiplied by itself, gives n: √49 = 7 because 7 × 7 = 49.
## ✏️ Example 1.8
List the first few multiples of 5, of 2 and of 4. Identify the perfect squares in each set.
**Solution**
| **Set** | **Elements** | **Perfect squares in the set** |
|---|---|---|
| Multiples of 5 | {5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, …} | {25, 100, 225, …} |
| Multiples of 2 | {2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, …} | {4, 16, 36, 64, …} |
| Multiples of 4 | {4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, 36, …} | {4, 16, 36, 64, …} |
The set of perfect squares is {1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, …}.
## Square roots by subtracting odd numbers
Every perfect square is the sum of consecutive odd numbers starting from 1: 1 = 1, 4 = 1 + 3, 9 = 1 + 3 + 5, 16 = 1 + 3 + 5 + 7, …
[[fig:m8-f02|Figure 1.1: Each square is built by adding the next odd number of tiles]]

pages.title: Example 1.9
pages.body:
## ✏️ Example 1.9
Use odd numbers to find √49.
**Solution**
Subtract consecutive odd numbers starting from 1 until the remainder is 0:
49 − 1 = 48; 48 − 3 = 45; 45 − 5 = 40; 40 − 7 = 33; 33 − 9 = 24; 24 − 11 = 13; 13 − 13 = 0
7 odd numbers were subtracted, so **√49 = 7**.
## ✏️ Example 1.10
Find √1,296 using prime factors.
**Solution**
1,296 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = (2 × 2 × 3 × 3) × (2 × 2 × 3 × 3) = 36 × 36
**√1,296 = 36**

pages.title: Union and intersection of sets
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Use knowledge of sets and sets of factors of numbers to solve real-life problems involving union and intersection.
Curriculum indicator B8.1.1.2.2
> 🔑 **Key idea: Union and intersection** — The **intersection** A ∩ B is the set of elements in **both** A and B. The **union** A ∪ B is the set of elements in A **or** B (or both). n(A) means the number of elements in A. For two sets: **n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)**.
## ✏️ Example 1.11
List the factors of 42 and 36 and find their common factors.
**Solution**
F₄₂ = {1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 14, 21, 42} F₃₆ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36}
F₄₂ ∩ F₃₆ = **{1, 2, 3, 6}** (the HCF is 6)
F₄₂ ∪ F₃₆ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 12, 14, 18, 21, 36, 42}
[[fig:m8-f03]]
Figure 1.2: Factors of 42 and 36
## ✏️ Example 1.12
There are 80 farmers in a village who grow maize, rice or both. 50 grow maize and 60 grow rice.
a) Represent the information on a Venn diagram. b) If x of them grow both crops, write an equation in x and solve it. c) How many grow only one crop?
**Solution**
a)
[[fig:m8-f04]]
Figure 1.3: Farmers growing maize and rice
b) Maize only = 50 − x; rice only = 60 − x. Every farmer is in one of the three regions:
(50 − x) + x + (60 − x) = 80 ⟹ 110 − x = 80 ⟹ **x = 30**
c) Maize only = 20, rice only = 30, so **50 farmers** grow only one crop.

pages.title: Chapter 1 summary
pages.body:
- Group digits in threes to read large numbers. Standard form: A × 10^{n}, 1 ≤ A < 10.
- Round to significant figures from the first non-zero digit; to decimal places after the point.
- Perfect squares: 1, 4, 9, 16, … ; the square root of n is the number whose square is n.
- A ∩ B: in both; A ∪ B: in either. n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).
